title: Ubisoft Massive Entertainment Boss Christoph Hartmann on His Amazon Games Exit and Turning ‘Splinter Cell’ Studio Into ‘A24 of Video Gaming’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Former Amazon Games chief Christoph Hartmann has been at the helm at Ubisoft‘s Massive Entertainment for five months and he’s now prepared to share
body:
Former Amazon Games chief Christoph Hartmann has been at the helm at Ubisoft‘s Massive Entertainment for five months and he’s now prepared to share his early vision for the future of the label behind Tom Clancy’s “The Division,” “Ghost Recon” and “Splinter Cell.”

	Those staple Ubisoft franchises, along with new IP “March of Giants,” a multiplayer online battle arena game Ubisoft acquired from Amazon (where it was previously developed by Hartmann and his team), and an unannounced game, are Hartmann’s main focus and part of his overall strategy to turn Massive Entertainment into the “A24 of video gaming” one day.
	

	“I want us to be two things,” Hartmann says. “I want us to be definitely not just a shooter house, which we show with having a mobile, besides the other titles. I want us to be a label which really looks after the core gamer. And what I mean by that, it’s almost easier to describe what we’re not going to do. So I’m not going to do a racing game. I’m not going to do sports. I’m not going to do a casual kids title. But could we do an RPG one day? Could we do MMO? Could I maybe do even a strategy game? Sure, it’s all coming down to the right talent. If we have the talent internally or something happens, then we bring it on.”

	See below for Variety‘s interview with Hartmann.
	
		Can you explain your exit from Amazon Games back in January and what led you to your new role at Ubisoft?	

	I worked basically in one company for 20 years, Take Two. I worked at Rockstar in the early days until “Grand Theft Auto: Vice City,” and then I formed 2K Games. But management was really self-taught. We knew how to make games and this and that. But growing the organization, I went to business school, but you don’t learn a lot about management, especially not the real world when you have to deal with humans and not just statistics. And I wanted to do something else and Amazon felt like a large company I can learn from how to do something. They wanted to focus on live services and I have a lot of experience with that and that’s why I joined them. And anything I really, really wanted to happen happened. 
	

	I learned so much about managing a large place, and I’m so grateful for it and it really helps me a lot. But it’s a while now, it’s seven years and at the end of the day, it’s a Big Tech company. And the tech industry is going through a massive transition right now. First of all, they have a lot of successful business they have to keep on running and then they have to focus on AI. Games just can’t be their prime focus right now. There’s so much going on. I’m just realistic about that. But for me, it’s the prime focus. I’m a content person. I’m not a tech person. I’m a content person. I love developing games. I love publishing games. That what gets me every day out of bed. I did that for 30 years and I’m just passionate about it. It means everything to me, and I felt I just need to go to a place again where it’s absolutely in the center of everything. And I think we have to be honest, Ubisoft definitely is one of those places. It’s still fully focused on games. I mean, they deeply, deeply care about it.
	
		What learnings did you bring over to Ubisoft from your time at Amazon?	

	Some of my colleagues at Amazon are gonna read it, they’re gonna laugh. But they have certain things in the culture, I was like, why are we doing that? You know, there’s that writing culture and now as I’m out, I’m like, “Oh my god, it was so good” because it ended up in a games company. You have more than open-ended two, three hours, blah blah blah blah blah and you can actually get to the point? Can actually come someone prepared and tell me what’s going on? I can make a decision. And we start doing that … That’s by the way, the beauty of offering a smaller business unit like Massive Entertainment because it enables us. We have a few layers of management we don’t have, so we can actually talk to people on the team. And there’s so much to be learned. That’s one thing I like and believe smaller organizations, especially in entertainment, are just very, very good.
	
		Ubisoft has acquired “March of Giants,” a game that was previously in development at Amazon. How did that deal come about?	

	“March of Giants,” that’s a team that came over to join me. They’re all “Rainbow Six Siege” people, some of the biggest best talents they had there and I’m very proud to have built that studio and I love those people dearly. And I was not involved in the decision or the deal in any form because Amazon really wanted to focus more on third-party development, AI rather than so much internal studios, so they did it. But once I started having conversation with Ubisoft, which happened, by the way, in a very natural way. I mean, I started my career 30 years ago in Europe. They distributed every single game in France and Europe for us. I actually published “Rainbow Six” in Europe before Ubisoft did. It’s just a small industry, you know each other. I almost felt like one day it’s gonna happen, but obviously that was a huge plus. I’m like, oh my god, I actually get to finish the game because there’s nothing I hate more than not to finish what we started.
	
	
		How do you see Massive Entertainment fitting into the larger Ubisoft and what it’s like working as the head of one of several Creative Houses?	

	It gives me the opportunity have a set of titles, a set of IPs, which you fit together. It fills the right package together, and I can build a new business, but don’t have to start from zero. So it’s kind of a dream come true for me. It’s just a company which cares about games. It just breaths games every day. And and to the question I kind of heard in there what I’m planning for massive entertainment. What it is, because I mean, you know, we have “The Division,” “Ghost Recon” and “Splinter Cell,” the new IPs, “March of Giants,” then we have another one in development with some great people, but I can’t announce it yet.

	And I want us to be two things. I want us to be definitely not just a shooter house, which we show with having a mobile, besides the other titles. I want us to be a label which really looks after the core gamer. And what I mean by that, it’s almost easier to describe what we’re not going to do. So I’m not going to do a racing game. I’m not going to do sports. I’m not going to do a casual kids title. But could we do an RPG one day? Could we do MMO? Could I maybe do even a strategy game? Sure, it’s all coming down to the right talent. If we have the talent internally or something happens, then we bring it on … Really my dream would be to become like the A24 of video gaming, like a place I describe with winning Oscars and still being commercially successful, definitely having impact on what they’re doing. It’s kind of the coolest place on planet Earth right now in you know a different industry, entertainment industry.

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

schema.headline: Ubisoft Massive Entertainment Boss Christoph Hartmann on His Amazon Games Exit and Turning ‘Splinter Cell’ Studio Into ‘A24 of Video Gaming’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Kin in the Game: How the Rise of Family Office Investors Is Reshaping Media, Entertainment and Sports
description: The dawn of Skydance — the film and TV leviathan that came forth from the biggest media acquisition in 25 years — was enabled by the most influentia
body:
The dawn of Skydance — the film and TV leviathan that came forth from the biggest media acquisition in 25 years — was enabled by the most influential trend in private investment in a decade: the rise of the family office investor.

	“Family office” is cuddly financial jargon for a specific form of holding company that ultrarich people and their relatives rely on to manage their wealth. The proliferation of near billionaires — and billionaires proper — in the U.S. since the stock market boom began in the 1980s has led to the creation of thousands of well-endowed family offices. “The size of this is extraordinary,” says Ian D’Souza, clinical professor of finance at the NYU Stern School of Business. “A lot of people don’t realize just how big they are as an investor class in a global context and their different risk-return drivers.”
	

	Family offices are gaining a level of clout that is having a profound impact on the ownership of media and entertainment assets. Many operate with a low profile — they don’t have the same financial disclosure requirements as other companies and investment firms. Among the most powerful entities flexing financial muscle is Lawrence Investments, the office that handles the prodigious fortune amassed by 82-year-old Larry Ellison, co-founder of software giant Oracle. Ellison is the father of Skydance chairman and CEO David Ellison, the mastermind of Skydance’s quest to bolt together studio and network assets. 

	The younger Ellison’s one-two punch began last year with his $8 billion acquisition of Paramount and CBS. And then he went in dogged pursuit of Warner Bros., HBO, CNN, Discovery and numerous other channels. It all culminated in the closing of the $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery transaction on Oct. 6. David Ellison couldn’t have pulled off those head-spinning deals without the full faith and credit backing of the enormous Ellison family wealth held through Lawrence Investments, which has an estimated $160 billion in assets under management. But Ellison’s empire-building boom has been financed with debt.
	

	The enlarged Skydance is carrying $80 billion in red ink, and if Skydance doesn’t make its aggressive debt and cost-reduction targets over the next three years, Larry Ellison will personally be on the hook for as much as $40 billion in debt payments to lenders. That’s how far the software mogul, who recently became a major shareholder in the U.S. spinoff of TikTok, went to help finance his son’s Hollywood ambition.

	As demonstrated by the Ellison family’s big swing, the influence of family office owners and investors will be markedly different from that of traditional private equity investors, experts say. Among the key differences:


Family office investors typically invest for the long term. They’re not under the pressure that private equity firms face to sell the company or mount a successful IPO after seven to 10 years.
They bring expertise to the table, investing in sectors and companies they know well.
Because family office firms don’t have to answer to shareholders, they have the freedom to pursue “trophy” investments that are seen as burnishing an individual’s or family’s legacy, such as full ownership or partial stakes in sports teams and high-profile entertainment properties.
They typically don’t have to disclose financial results to anyone beyond their core insiders because they usually don’t take on outside partners or publicly traded debt.



	According to data analysis from global investor research firm Altss, the number of family offices has grown at a rate of nearly 5% a year, culminating in more than 8,000 firms managing as much as $5 trillion or more in assets. The top 50 firms have an estimated $2.4 trillion in assets under management; the top 10 alone account for $1.5 trillion.



	

									Kelsey Dake for Variety
	



	Generally speaking, it takes about $250 million in seed money to launch a large single-investor family office. Others are formed with $50 million to $100 million, and sometimes a handful of those firms will join together in a multi-family office. One of the biggest of those is Iconiq Capital, which handles some personal investing for Mark Zuckerberg, Sheryl Sandberg, Jack Dorsey and Linkedin co-founder Reid Hoffman, among others.

	The reigning company among family offices remains Walton Enterprises, the $225 billion colossus controlled by the heirs of Walmart founder Sam Walton. Elon Musk, the entrepreneur behind Tesla and SpaceX, funnels some of his personal investments through his Excession family office, valued at $200 billion. Bill Gates’ Cascade Investment is another heavyweight at $170 billion. Amazon pioneer Jeff Bezos holds his roughly 9% stake in the e-commerce giant (which encompasses Amazon MGM Studios and Prime Video) through his Bezos Expeditions office, with an estimated $107 billion in assets under management.

	“The ability to create wealth over a short period of time right now is incredible, and because of that, all of a sudden you’ve got someone like Elon buying Twitter and turning it into what he wanted it to be,” says Greg Suess, co-founder and head of Activist Artists Management’s family office practice. “It was unfathomable that you would see an individual be able to buy a company of that size on his own. But that is the way it is now. A lot of these family offices are of the size where they can take swings on major entertainment assets. That has shocked the industry.”
	

	At the same time, fortunes the size of Ellison’s, Musk’s and the Walton clan’s are still outliers — the 1% of the 1%. The more pervasive impact is coming from the many other family offices steered by less than astronomically wealthy people who are drawn to the soft power of media. Think Steve Sarowitz, the payroll-software billionaire whose Illinois-based 4S Bay Partners family office teamed with Justin Baldoni to launch “It Ends With Us” production company Wayfarer Studios.

	David Steward II has also inherited significant wealth from his father, World Wide Technology co-founder David Steward. The younger Steward in recent years has invested in comic-book imprints and the Lion Forge Entertainment animation studio with the goal of bringing more diverse stories to life as family animation films. The Steward family has also worked with NASCAR and Richard Petty Motorsports to sponsor the groundbreaking driver Bubba Wallace, and it was an owner of the family’s hometown NHL team, the St. Louis Blues, from 2012 until selling the stake in 2024.

	“Our mission is very much around what we call diverse stories authentically told. It’s about displaying and telling stories from varied backgrounds, whether it be racial, socioeconomic or gender,” the younger Steward says. “We’re a lot more patient with outcomes because we have a higher vision. We’re not only investing to get a return; we’re investing for change. We’re investing in people at the end of the day. So it’s a different kind of philosophy as we look at those things.

	“There are three pillars to any family office that I’ve ever been around,” says Edward Hamati, a wealth management pro who is chief investment officer for the Steward Trust and the Steward Family Office. “Trust, treasury and banking — that’s one bucket. Building the corpus, that’s another bucket. Anyone can give you 50 ways that you do that. And then there’s the third bucket, which is, What is this family about and what do we have to care about because of the family? What are they motivated by? What do the kids want? Is there a lot of family politics? You have to think through all that around any family you work with.”

	Joe Becher, CAA’s global managing partner and founder of its executive search practice, has felt the same demand that spurred Suess and partners to form Activist. Becher expanded CAA into family office specialty services as he found himself conducting C-suite searches for firms that had been bought out by family offices.
	

	“Probably two to three years ago we started seeing this trend of family offices popping up everywhere, whether it be in media companies or music-catalog businesses or sports franchises,” Becher says. “Very often, instead of us dealing with an owner in isolation or a private equity firm with institutional capital, we were dealing with family offices. They needed our help to understand the assets that they’ve invested in. They needed our help to structure them the right way and build the right operating teams.”

	Traditionally, the family office investment model was associated with vintage American family fortunes such as the oil money of the Rockefellers or the publishing and media empires of William Randolph Hearst and E.W. Scripps. Hearst and Scripps still operate as well-established media companies. But their governance structure makes them essentially family offices that are run by trusted staffers who ensure that the generational wealth keeps flowing to heirs for decades to come.

	But nothing has animated the family office sector lately like the availability of sports teams and music catalogs. The latter is seen as a form of timeless physical media that will retain value no matter how much music consumption changes in the streaming era. On the other hand, sports franchise deals are usually driven by raw passion and bragging rights.

	“There’s only so many of them, and so that sense of paying for scarcity and legacy impact are important drivers for family offices that don’t really exist for other types of pooled capital because they have a time-duration problem,” D’Souza says. Some first-generation wealth generators thrive on the challenge of turning around properties like sports teams or rehabilitating beloved fashion or retail brands. “They feel like, ‘I made it once; I can do it again,’” says D’Souza, who has served as a board member for numerous family offices over the years.

	At best, a family office can bring to the table resources and in some cases synergies with other holdings for an acquisition. Steward II notes that the company’s work with NASCAR and driver Wallace led to World Wide Technology upgrading the racing circuit’s digital infrastructure to help it make the most of AI and other cutting-edge tech.

	Steward II emphasizes that the company can’t completely ignore financial results. But it has the luxury of options. “We do have the investments that are a little bit colder and distant and more financially oriented. And then we have this entrepreneurial pile, and in that pile comes [ideas] by way of passion and by way of utilizing the relationships that we have,” Steward says. “Everything we’ve done in sports and entertainment has been led by those two things. We want to see change in the industry as well. So how can we best not only put our creative foot forward, but how can we leverage our relationships for change as well?”
	

	The flood of investment and financing dollars flowing into a broad range of industry deals in recent years has turned the private investment vehicles of the ultra-high-net-worth crowd into the most courted players in global investing. “It has become recognized that families are more viable owners of various assets than they were considered to be in the past,” Activist’s Suess says. “The wealth has grown so much. They’ve become business rock stars.”

	(Pictured top: Family office investors Gigi Pritzker, Steve Sarowitz, David Steward II and François-Henri Pinault)

schema.headline: Kin in the Game: How the Rise of Family Office Investors Is Reshaping Media, Entertainment and Sports

title: Harrison Ford Exec-Produced Voyaging Film ‘The Navigator’ Unveils Clip Ahead of DOC NYC Premiere (EXCLUSIVE)
description: “The Navigator,” a voyaging film directed by Jordan Manley and executive produced by Harrison Ford, has unveiled an exclusive clip ahead of its Nov
body:
“The Navigator,” a voyaging film directed by Jordan Manley and executive produced by Harrison Ford, has unveiled an exclusive clip ahead of its Nov. 19 East Coast bow at DOC NYC.

	Ford also supplied a message with the clip.

	“‘The Navigator’ is a deeply moving film – one I’m truly grateful for. Its powerful storytelling and cinematic beauty left me in awe. Master navigator Nainoa Thompson, his teachers, and his students are extraordinary examples of profound humility. They help us understand why ancient wisdom matters in a modern world, and remind us what we are capable of when we act in harmony with nature,” Ford said.
	

	Ford is one of seven executive producers on the project, a group that also includes Yvon Chouinard and Laurene Powell Jobs. Kathy Thompson and Laura Yale are the producers, and Yo-Yo Ma contributes cello to a score by Matthew Robert Cooper.

	The film’s world premiere took place Oct. 21 at Hawaiʻi Theater on Oʻahu during the Hawaii International Film Festival, and it left with the Pacific Awards – Feature prize. Thompson, meanwhile, received the Halekulani Legacy Award.

	In 1980, Thompson crossed from Hawai’i to Tahiti by voyaging canoe using neither a compass nor modern instruments, becoming the first Native Hawaiian to do so in six centuries.

	Now nearly 50 years later, he is making the crossing again, for what the film presents as the last time. Thompson sails with a handful of student navigators. They rely on the stars, natural cues and the lessons of the late Mau Piailug, a master navigator, along a 2,400-mile route their ancestors sailed. Piailug, who was raised on Satawal in Micronesia, taught Native Hawaiians traditional navigation.
	

	Manley said in a director’s statement: “I came to see a deep burden and ‘kuleana’ that rests upon the shoulders of Nainoa Thompson, who has spent the last 50 years of his life fulfilling a promise made to his teacher, Micronesian master navigator Mau Piailug, to prevent navigation from going extinct.”

	The director, based in Vancouver, previously made “Treeline” and the series “A Skier’s Journey.” Submarine is handling sales and distribution inquiries.

title: Royal Family Embraces Robert Pattinson’s 007 Casting: ‘Welcome to His Majesty’s Secret Service, Mr. Bond’
description:
Robert Pattinson‘s casting as James Bond has received a nod of polite acknowledgement from the British monarchy.

	Roughly 90 minutes after the new
body:
Robert Pattinson‘s casting as James Bond has received a nod of polite acknowledgement from the British monarchy.

	Roughly 90 minutes after the news broke that Pattinson was to lead Amazon MGM Studios reboot of the hit franchise, the royals joined hundreds of thousands of commentators on social media — but did so in a manner that really only they could. 

	“Welcome to His Majesty’s Secret Service, Mr Bond,” they posted on the royal family‘s official X account, with a link to the announcement.
	

	As it happens, Pattinson will be the very first Bond to work for His Majesty’s Secret Service rather than Her Majesty’s Secret Service. Queen Elizabeth II was monarch across the entire slate of 25 titles until her passing in 2022, a year after the release of “No Time to Die,” the last 007 movie and Daniel Craig’s final stint as the super spy.


	Pattinson’s casting brought to a close years of speculation over who incoming Bond director Denis Villenueve would hand the famed Walther PKK, speculation that turned into a frenzy over the last month as the names were whittled down. Jacob Elordi was initially a favorite for the role in the earliest days, but reports later surfaced that the “Euphoria” star didn’t even screen test for the part. Jack Lowden then entered the fray, with his “Slow Horses” co-star Gary Oldman sparking headlines when he claimed Bond was already picked and cheekily added that his “fingers are crossed” for Lowden. Callum Turner spent a lengthy period as a candidate on many lips and was reportedly down to the final stages. But then the tables were turned at the 11th hour when it emerged broke that both Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult had auditioned. 
	

	“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement. “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

schema.headline: Royal Family Embraces Robert Pattinson’s 007 Casting: ‘Welcome to His Majesty’s Secret Service, Mr. Bond’

title: ‘The Odyssey’ Cinematographer Hoyte Van Hoytema Breaks Down Filming Climactic Thunderstorm Scene in Imax
description: Christopher Nolan shot “The Odyssey” to be experienced on the biggest screen possible so audiences could feel the full impact and be fully immersed
body:
Christopher Nolan shot “The Odyssey” to be experienced on the biggest screen possible so audiences could feel the full impact and be fully immersed in that experience — so everything was shot practically. 

	One of the most challenging sequences to pull off was the film’s final storm scene as Matt Damon’s Odysseus faces the wrath of Poseidon and the full force of Zeus. It was to be climactic and intense, and Odysseus loses all his men as a result of the final insult to the gods.
	

	“We had been talking about going out there to sea, sit on real boats and shoot on Imax,” cinematographer Hoyte Van Hoytema explains. 

	A large amount of the film was shot on the open ocean, where Nolan, his cast and crew spent four months capturing how hard the journey would have been as they endured crashing waves. And while the climactic moment ended up being shot in Los Angeles, Nolan didn’t spare any expense in pulling off the sequence, relying instead on old-fashioned filmmaking.Speaking with Variety for Inside the Frame, Van Hoytema explains the scene provided a challenge: “How to replicate something and make it feel visceral and real? How can we do that and avoid a huge amount of CG?”Two decommissioned jet engines were used as wind machines. Van Hoytema’s chief lighting technician and gaffer Adam Chambers built light boxes that would emulate thunder and lightning. The boat was then put on a gimbal, all while being shot on an Imax camera. “It was like shooting a real storm, just under safety supervision,” Van Hoytema says.He adds, “We did a lot of different setups in that whole scene. It is designed to feel extremely chaotic; it’s designed to sort of not understand really what’s going on.”The lighting design was something he also had to think about. “It was interesting because I was thinking, if you’re out at sea at night 2,000 years ago, without electricity and you end up in a thunderstorm, what would that feel like? I was thinking, if you can see everything around you, that’s going to look fake.”

	A CGI storm didn’t feel right because the entire crew had been meticulous about keeping everything as grounded and as experiential as possible. Van Hoytema says the team built overhead lighting rigs that were approximately 60×30 feet, hanging on cranes above the ship. “It meant that you would see flashes that progressively move from behind them to the front of them, as it opens up the sky. “What you see is short bursts and there’s just darkness or a little bit of a glow. It’s like trying to see this relentless endless sea, this weather, this saltwater and they’re just so close to death. It’s extremely claustrophobic at the same time.”

	When it came to framing Odysseus, Van Hoytema was wired in to keep him in place on the gimbal. His Imax camera on his shoulder was also wired in.

	“I was not trying to be in any way precious about framing whatsoever. I was just trying through with a jet engine blowing, gallons of water in my face. I was literally just trying to identify if it was even Matt Damon in the shot. It was extremely visceral, and it’s almost hard to grasp. It was not a situation in which you could just start a take or not. Every take was an event.”
	

	Van Hoytema says the camera starts to roll and the jet engines start. “They rise, and at some point, they sound like two fighter jets are next to your ear. And it gets really wild because they start moving the gimbal as well, and you’re holding on for your life. The camera gets turned; it’s the original Imax camera, not the blimp and the Imax camera is very loud. However, in that situation, you don’t even know if it’s turned on. You do a take, and you have a crazy powerful adrenaline rush.”

	In contrast, Van Hoytema recalled a moment when the crew was out to sea, in open waters and a pod of bottlenose dolphins appeared. It was completely unplanned.

	Van Hoytema recalls, “It’s interesting because it was also pretty violent that day. It was very harsh weather and I remember a lot of people on the crew got seasick. As we started filming, dolphins started to jump out of the water. What is interesting is that it symbolizes that no matter what the weather does, we take the weather as it comes and accept it as the reality you work in that day.”

schema.headline: ‘The Odyssey’ Cinematographer Hoyte Van Hoytema Breaks Down Filming Climactic Thunderstorm Scene in Imax

title: Shondaland Hires Amy Joy Rivkin as VP of Production, Karyn Smith-Forge Hired as VP of Scripted Series
description: Shondaland has brought on Amy Jo Rivkin in the role of vice president of production, with Karyn Smith-Forge joining the company as vice president o
body:
Shondaland has brought on Amy Jo Rivkin in the role of vice president of production, with Karyn Smith-Forge joining the company as vice president of scripted series. 

	“Amy Joy’s impressive track record steering complex, premium productions and Karyn’s vast experience and sharp instincts across scripted genres make them powerful additions to Shondaland,” said Alison Eakle, Shondaland’s chief content officer. “We’re thrilled we get to shape our next chapter of storytelling alongside them.” 
	

	Rivkin will oversee physical production for Shondaland. Prior to joining the company, she worked at Michael Ellenberg’s Media Res for four years, where she also oversaw physical production on shows like “The Morning Show” for Apple TV. Prior to that, she worked in the Netflix original series, drama, group as well as at Legendary Entertainment.  

	Smith-Forge will lead development of new series at Shondaland under their expansive overall deal with Netflix. She was most recently the president of Don Cheadle’s production company, This Radicle Act Productions. She was also previously senior vice president of production for Berlanti Productions. 

	Shondaland has been based at Netflix since 2017. It was announced over the summer that the company would remain at the streamer for a further five years. In addition to serving as the exclusive home to Shondaland film and TV projects, the overall deal also covers gaming, merchandise, and live events connected to the IP.

	Shondaland’s biggest show to date on Netflix is “Bridgerton,” which aired its fourth season earlier this year and is currently prepping its fifth. It is one of the most popular show’s in Netflix history, with Seasons 1 and 3 ranking in the Top 10 Netflix shows of all time with 113 million views and 106 million views respectively. Along with the previous prequel about Queen Charlotte, Netflix recently greenlit a second “Bridgerton” prequel about a young Lady Violet.

schema.headline: Shondaland Hires Amy Joy Rivkin as VP of Production, Karyn Smith-Forge Hired as VP of Scripted Series

title: How Netflix‘s Animated ‘Steps’ Reimagines the Cinderella Story Through the Eyes of Her Asian Stepsisters and Finds a New Kind of Happily Ever After
description: Netflix’s animated feature “Steps” surface reboots the Cinderella tale: an orphan tormented by an evil stepmother and her loathsome daughters. But
body:
Netflix’s animated feature “Steps” surface reboots the Cinderella tale: an orphan tormented by an evil stepmother and her loathsome daughters. But this tale, directed by Alyce Tzue and John Ripa, turns that legend upside-down, offering a revisionist history of what really happened — and it has nothing to do with horrible steps, but everything to do with fear, othering and mean girls, with some magic of course.

	Set in the kingdom of Alouette, the story begins with two little girls, Lilith and Margot, moving into their stepfather’s home and becoming fast friends with his little girl, Cinderella. Everybody’s happy until Cinderella sides with the mean girls at a party, and their father dies. Lilith turns rebellious, because why not? The whole town kinda hates her because she’s different anyway — she, Margot and mom are Asian. Blonde Cinderella talks to animals, cleans, sings and everyone loves her. But while the story follows the  familiar contours — there’s a fairy godmother and a prince, of course — “Steps” takes many twists in an entertaining and illuminating journey. Film’s voice cast stars Ali Wong, Amanda Seyfried, Stephanie Hsu, Bette Midler, Daniel Radcliffe, Young Manzino and Nikki Glaser.
	

	The first animated feature from Amy Poehler’s Paper Kite, the film looks luscious, like a tempting birthday cake or candy.

	Tzue had been working on the film for seven years. Comedians and writers Ricki Lindhome and Kate Micucci of Garfunkel and Oates had a concept that they worked together on with Paper Kite, says Tzue, and brought it to Netflix. “There was this idea of a movie from the stepsisters’ perspective. It was a very different movie,” says the director. “They were white stepsisters, and they were more the canonically mean girls that you might expect and they sent the script to me to check it out. And I thought it had just like this sharply feminist message, and as well as these values of inclusivity and sisterhood that really grabbed me. And so I pitched to both Paper Kite and Netflix, and I got the job to direct it.”
	

	But Tzue saw parallels to her young life in the story as the film took a different direction.

	“I will say that my Taiwanese and Chinese ethnicity is a deep part of who I am, and it has made me into the artist and filmmaker that I am. I’m proud of it, and growing up in a pretty homogeneous small town, it has also caused me to feel different,” she says. “And I think one being making the stepsisters Asian allowed me to give them this nuance and specificity and vulnerability that can be informed from my own experience.”

	She adds: “I felt like there were just these parallels between my experience and Lilith’s experience. Just like Cinderella fits this archetype of a fairy tale protagonist, and Lilith doesn’t. I also felt like the girls I grew up with were, you know, meant to find this traditional kind of happiness and they’re happy ever after. And I felt like I was too different to find that myself. It was this effort to tell stories about what I know and the personal journey that I’m so close to.”

	Tzue says, “My directing partner John Ripa and I feel like we will have done our jobs if even one person walks away feeling like they can stand up for someone else.”

	Veteran animator Ripa joined the production a little later than Tzue, but they immediately vibed on the film’s themes. He wanted to find out “what she wanted to say with it because what she wanted to say comes from her experiences growing up and talking about wanting everybody to see themselves in the fairy tale, everybody deserving a happy happily ever after and the idea of empathy and kindness. And for me, I felt like that was very universal. And I felt like that was really important, especially in the world today. And so, I really locked into what Alice wanted to say with it and that was kind of like my driving force too.”

	The Rococo Alouette was also a character. “This kingdom of conformists that wouldn’t accept any difference, right? And we wanted to play into that idea as well,” she says

	There’s original songs, lots of gags — including one about the prince’s face blindness — scary villain chases and of course, a glass carriage and slippers.

	She quips that Cinderella purists might not like this version of the story but she and the team had “fun of playing around with fairy tale tropes, trying to see what world lies beyond this kingdom of Alouette. There’s an enchanted forest, and also comes with it these trolls that live under bridges and ride motorcycles, but really, I think what we’re trying to do is bring it thematically back to this idea of who’s included in the fairy tale and who isn’t. You know, in our world, the trolls aren’t, which gives ‘Steps’ this room to grow into or it gives Alouette room to grow into the kingdom that we kind of wish it were by the end.”
	

	The look is bright, saturated color, gleaming and dreamy. It almost looks toylike. The animators’ intent was to draw in the audience with the colors and the miniaturization.

	“I come from a CG background, and I’ve loved working with CG as a 3D medium in particular,” Tzue, who started out as an architect, says. “From architecture to working as a CG generalist, I’ve loved things like surfacing and lighting and while I love the movies that have 3D emulate 2D — they look beautiful — I really wanted to push 3D to feel even more 3D.”

	“Especially in terms of the world, the fabrics, the textures, just how kind of rich and ornate and how everything was kind of really constructed. It was like a big part of the look of the film that you know we wanted to do because it’s one of the things that CG does best,” says Ripa. “It can add these textures and freckles and to this ornate Rococo world. But then you have to take it and make sure that the audience is seeing and feeling what they’re supposed to see and feel, because if you let it take over, you can lose emotion in connection with the characters. So, we were trying to make sure, even in the complexity of it, that the characters and the emotions were still at the at the forefront.”



	

									Netflix Animation Studios

title: Berlin Winner Tatiana Huezo Close to Completing Road Movie ‘Galerna’ Following Awards Boost: ‘I’m Dying to Finish It’
description: Mexican-Salvadoran director Tatiana Huezo is inching close to finishing “Galerna,” her follow-up to the Berlinale-winning documentary “The Echo.” T
body:
Mexican-Salvadoran director Tatiana Huezo is inching close to finishing “Galerna,” her follow-up to the Berlinale-winning documentary “The Echo.” The film, which has been brewing for the last three years, is fresh off market wins at both San Sebastián and Morelia, giving the director a major boost ahead of her time at IDFA as this year’s Guest of Honor.

	Speaking with Variety out of the Amsterdam festival and following a lengthy career discussion moderated by IDFA artistic director Isabel Arrate Fernandez, Huezo says her second fiction film (following 2021’s lauded “Prayers for the Stolen”) feels like a “breached child.” It’s a film that was stopped for a little while due to lack of financing, and I call it a breached child because the culmination of this filmmaking journey, the premiere, feels like a birth. It’s like seeing a child be born and finally walking alone.”
	

	“Galerna” trails casting directors Lúa (Ilse Salas) and Noé (Lázaro Gabino Rodríguez), whose latest job is to find natural actors for a sci-fi movie. They are working together for the first time, with Noé coming from the countryside and Lúa an unemployed actress from the big city. The duo travels together to remote areas in Mexico, staying in the houses of welcoming strangers along the way. In this road trip, they encounter a country that simultaneously embraces them and makes them confront their fears and prejudices.

	“This film was held up because we took the risk of shooting without consolidated financing,” adds the director. “We were also very dependent on the weather and several other uncontrollable circumstances.” “Galerna” was shot in Juchitán in the South of Mexico and the northern desert of Chihuahua. “It’s a journey, a road movie.”
	

	Asked about why she decided to take “Galerna” to several markets over the last two years, Huezo emphasizes both the financial aspect of meeting investors and the possibility of getting peer feedback. “We had the opportunity to go to San Sebastián’s works-in-progress showcase to look for money. I was very apprehensive because you don’t ever know what you have until you share it with others. I am always very afraid. Every time I make a film, it feels like the first time.”

	“Every film is a leap into the void, where you have to reinvent yourself, considering all the risks involved and relying on a deep desire to tell a story,” she goes on. “That’s how I experience filmmaking. I never take on a project where I can say everything is perfectly under control and I know exactly what the results will be. For me, every film is incredibly intense, and I never know how it will turn out.”



	

					Tatiana Huezo and Isabel Arrate Fernandez at IDFA, courtesy of Roger Cremers
									Roger Cremers
	



	The director notes how “financing independent cinema is always difficult.” “It’s important to mention that the primary source of funding for this film comes from EFICINE, a state fund that supports Mexican independent cinema. It has been absolutely essential. Without that support, Mexican cinema simply wouldn’t exist. Thanks to the fund, we were able to get the initial phase of production underway, but this is a very complex and ambitious film.”

	But the real “turning point” for “Galerna” was being part of San Sebastián’s WIP Latam section. “The film resonated beautifully with people there. It stirred deep emotions and sparked a great deal of curiosity.”

	“Galerna” won the coveted EGEDA Platino Industria Award worth €30,000 ($33,000) at the festival, which the director credits with drawing the interest of other investors and distributors. Right after the festival, Mexico’s Sula Films boarded the project, joining Pimienta Films (“Roma”) as a co-producer.

	“It was a realization that the film was alive,” she says. Huezo then took the project to Mexico’s Morelia Film Festival, where it snagged the top prize at Impulso Morelia, the WIP section of the event. “The film really took off from there, thankfully, and reaffirmed my belief that these leaps into the unknown are absolutely worth taking.”
	

	“Right now, we’re in the final stages of production,” she says. “I’m here at [IDFA], caught in a whirlwind with a packed schedule, while simultaneously navigating the very intense final push to complete the film. I’m working with musicians, the sound designer, and finalizing the edit. It’s all coming together in a great swirl of activity to bring ‘Galerna’ to life. I’m dying to finish it and finally bring this child of mine into the world.”

	Lastly, the filmmaker briefly spoke about the “wonderful” sense of hope brought to Latin American politics following Lula’s presidential victory in Brazil last month. “Lula’s victory was like a brilliant light at the end of a dark tunnel; it brought a major shift in perspective in Latin America. It signalled that we are still here; we still have the possibility of resisting, of fighting for democracy together.”

	“There was this heavy sense of darkness blanketing the entire world, a wave of fascism, the rise of the far-right, something truly formidable and profoundly dark,” she adds. “I feel that Lula’s victory shifted the landscape in a very significant way, not just in Mexico but globally. There are crazy, deranged people in power today in Latin America. People who are extremely dangerous and who are completely and utterly removed from anything human, but right now, I’m feeling hopeful.”

title: ‘Hunger Games’ Costume Designer Teams With Depop on Vintage Fashion Collection, Including Edits for Effie and Haymitch
description:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Depop is
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Depop is bringing the fashion of Panem to the resale market.

	Ahead of the Nov. 20 theatrical release of “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,” the secondhand fashion marketplace has teamed up with Lionsgate and the film’s costume designer, Bina Daigeler, on a series of shoppable edits inspired by four of the prequel’s central characters.

	Launching Monday, the collaboration features curated selections of vintage and secondhand clothing inspired by Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak), Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace) and Effie Trinket (Elle Fanning). Rather than producing new merchandise, the partnership draws on existing inventory from independent Depop sellers.
	

	The four edits reflect the film’s mix of 1970s fashion, romantic silhouettes and theatrical Capitol style. Haymitch’s rebellious, rock-inspired wardrobe looks like worn-in leather jackets, patchwork button-downs, corduroy pants and workwear boots, while Lenore Dove’s Western-influenced bohemian look includes flowing maxi dresses, lace and cowboy boots. Maysilee’s vintage glamour comes through in 1960s-inspired halter dresses, satin skirts and opera gloves, while Effie’s more extravagant aesthetic features floral prints, corsets, statement jewelry and playful headpieces.


						
			
	

	
					

	“Clothes help tell a character’s story through silhouette, texture, color and the way pieces are combined,” Daigeler said in a statement. “Collaborating with Depop is an opportunity to share those details with fans and invite them to interpret the characters’ styles in their own way. Vintage and secondhand pieces bring their own history and individuality to that process.”
	

	“Pop culture is a huge source of inspiration for the Depop community, with reverberations that help shape what happens next in fashion,” said Steve Dool, Depop’s senior director of brand and creative. “Whether someone connects with Haymitch’s leather jackets or Effie’s eclectic accessories, these Depop x Hunger Games edits offer a starting point to translate these indelible film wardrobe staples into a modern, personal way of expressing yourself.”

	Directed by Francis Lawrence and adapted from Suzanne Collins’ 2025 novel, “Sunrise on the Reaping” takes place 24 years before the events of the original “Hunger Games,” following a young Haymitch as he is selected to compete in the 50th Hunger Games, also known as the Second Quarter Quell. The film marks the sixth installment in Lionsgate’s blockbuster franchise, following 2023’s “The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes,” and features an ensemble cast including Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Kieran Culkin, Glenn Close and Maya Hawke.

	The Depop x “Hunger Games” edits are available through the marketplace’s website and app in the U.S. and Australia from Nov. 16 through Nov. 29.

title: Horror Host Joe Bob Briggs Launches Coney Island Pictures With Picturehouse; New ‘Basket Case’ Movie Among First Projects (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Joe Bob Briggs’ “The Last Drive-in” is coming to an end at Shudder this year, but he’s taking a bold new step that will thrill genre fans.

	Briggs
body:
Joe Bob Briggs’ “The Last Drive-in” is coming to an end at Shudder this year, but he’s taking a bold new step that will thrill genre fans.

	Briggs, along with distributor and producer Bob Berney, announced the creation of Coney Island Pictures today, Variety can exclusively reveal. The horror-focused production and distribution company will have worldwide distribution from Picturehouse, Berney’s distribution and marketing company.
	

	“I’ve known Bob since the ’80s, when the two of us were rooming together at the Cannes Film Festival to save money and collaborating on weird film festivals at the only real arthouse in Dallas,” Briggs said in a statement. “Bob went off to Hollywood, distributed the two most successful indie films in history, marketed movies worth a billion in box office, many of them winning Academy Awards, and developed friendships with the top directors in the business, while I was writing books about exploitation movies and hosting ‘The Night Evelyn Came Out of the Grave’ at 1 a.m. on cable. Our two worlds eventually collided through what I call the Horror Renaissance of 2016. Bob’s friend Guillermo del Toro won the Academy Award, and AMC Networks launched the Shudder streaming service, where I would spend almost a decade putting the trivia embedded in the back of my brain to work.”

	“I’ve known Joe Bob since I owned the Inwood Theater and he was the film critic at the Dallas Times Herald,” Berney, Picturehouse’s CEO, also said in a statement. “Together, in the early ’90s, we screened both classic and unknown genre films with special guest stars and tributes. The status of horror has been greatly elevated in today’s marketplace, and Coney Island Pictures is uniquely situated to acquire and produce a new generation of films with the added advantage of being able to talk directly to the fans of Joe Bob Briggs. It’s something we’ve always wanted to do and the time is right.”
	

	Per the presser, Coney Island’s first projects include “a dark horror comedy, a new version of a classic horror paperback, and a reimagining of the 1981 cult horror classic ‘Basket Case’ in collaboration with original director Frank Henenlotter.”

	Anthony Sneed, Henenlotter’s longtime creative partner and protégé, will direct the adaptation.

	“I sponsored the world premiere of the original ‘Basket Case’ at the Highway 183 Drive-In in Irving, Texas,” Briggs also said. “Bob helped me promote it with the World Drive-In Movie Festival. Now, decades later, we’re working with its original creator, Frank Henenlotter. Because every generation needs a ‘Basket Case!’”

	Berney and Briggs will serve as co-CEOs of the company. Picturehouse’s Jeanne R. Berney will serve as head of marketing, and former Explorers Club media executive Austin Raywood will serve as head of production.

	Briggs is best known for his decades of presenting and discussing horror films on television. His show “Joe Bob’s Drive-in Theater” aired on The Movie Channel from 1986 to 1996, his TNT series “MonsterVision” ran from 1996 to 2000 and “The Last Drive-in with Joe Bob Briggs” debuted on Shudder in 2018 and is wrapping up this year.

title: Student Pilot Who Was in the Air During FAA Ground Stop Speaks Out
description:
Viral Student Pilot
                          Ground Stop Was A First For All Of Us
body:
Viral Student Pilot
                          Ground Stop Was A First For All Of Us
                          ... 'This Does Not Happen'
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 16, 2026
                            8:00 AM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The student pilot who told an air traffic controller he straight-up didn't know what to do when the nationwide ground stop was declared ultimately landed safely ... and he confirmed he never discussed the scenario with his instructor -- because it "does not happen."
      
    
            CBS News caught up with Mosab Nadi ... the Texas-based student pilot who was making his first solo cross-country flight when Friday's FAA ground stop went into effect.
      
    
            Audio from the call between him and air traffic control went viral ... which he says surprised him -- noting the whole situation was unique.
      

            Mosab says the situation seemingly changed rapidly ... he says he'd been on the phone with ATC mere minutes before, and there had been no ground stop. Suddenly, he was being told to land.
      
    
            Thankfully, Mosab says he felt confident in his ability to safely put the plane on the ground ... though he notes the feeling when he finally landed was "unimaginable."
      
    
            He adds, "This does not happen at all. It's not even something that I talked about with my instructor." 
      
    
            While he ended up in a frightening situation, Mosab says he can't wait to get back up in the air for another cross-country flight.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            It's good he's gone through this trial by fire ... because government officials -- like Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy -- say this is likely to happen again.
      
    
            Duffy pointed to a faulty router as the culprit ... while President Donald Trump pointed the finger at his predecessor Joe Biden.

                                                                        Published

                            6:44 AM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 16, 2026
                                7:31 AM PST
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Gypsy Rose Blanchard's former fiancé, Ken Urker, died from a heroin overdose ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            The Lafourche Parish Coroner's Office tells TMZ ... Ken's death was ruled an accident, with his official cause of death listed as polysubstance drug toxicity -- meaning a combination of drugs caused a fatal reaction. The medical examiner later confirmed fentanyl was in Ken's system when he died. 
      
    
            We broke the story ... Gypsy's brother, Dylan Blanchard, found Ken dead in his bed on what would've been his 34th birthday on Oct. 1.
      

            Cops say drug paraphernalia -- including syringes and a spoon -- was found near his body, as was a brown powdery substance. They also say a holstered handgun was found on the nightstand.
      
    
            Gypsy told us shortly after Ken died that an overdose was suspected ... though she also said she didn't know he had a drug problem.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Deputies say they were told Ken went to church with members of the Blanchard family the night before his death and made comments about being depressed and upset.
      
    
            Gypsy and Ken had hit a rough patch before his passing ... taking time apart, though sources say they were not broken up or even on a break. We were told his drinking created a strain on their relationship.
      
    
            Gypsy and Ken share one child, a daughter named Aurora.
      
    
            After Gypsy and Aurora attended a private viewing of Ken's body in Louisiana on Oct. 4 ... Ken's family -- all of whom get along with Gyspsy aside from Ken's sister Autumn -- invited her to his Texas funeral.
      
    
            Just recently ... Gypsy spoke out again about his death, saying she believed with "100% certainty" that he did not die by suicide.
